# Overview

This document contains additional figures exploring the characteristics of the spawner-recruitment relationships for 356 Pacific salmon populations throughout the Northeast Pacific region.


```{r load,  include=FALSE}
library(here);library(ggplot2);library(dplyr);library(cowplot);library(ggspatial);library(sf);library(rnaturalearth);library(pheatmap);library(cmdstanr)
options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE)
stock_dat<- read.csv(here('data','salmon_productivity_compilation2026-08-10.csv'))
stock_dat$stock=gsub('/','_',stock_dat$stock)
stock_dat$stock=gsub('&','and',stock_dat$stock)
stock_info<- read.csv(here('data','stock_info2026-08-10.csv'))
#Remove stocks with less than 15 years of recruitment data
stock_info$stock.name=gsub('/','_',stock_info$stock.name)
stock_info$stock.name=gsub('&','and',stock_info$stock.name)

stock_info$state=factor(stock_info$state,levels=c('WA','BC','AK'))
stock_info$ocean.basin=factor(stock_info$ocean.basin,levels=c('SC','NC','GoA','BS'))

stock_dat2=subset(stock_dat,stock.id %in% stock_info$stock.id)
#length(unique(stock_dat2$stock)) #267
stock_dat2$logR_S=log(stock_dat2$recruits/stock_dat2$spawners)

stock_info$species2=gsub("-.*", "", stock_info$species) # collapse even/odd pinks together

stk.info=stock_info
chk.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Chinook')
scy.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Sockeye')
chm.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Chum')
cho.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Coho')
pke.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Pink-Even')
pko.info=subset(stock_info,species=='Pink-Odd')

```

## Fig. S2. Ratio of Capacity (Smax) to maximum observed spawners

For our Bayesian hierarchical models, we used informative priors to estimate stock production capacitiy, $S_{max}$, based on the maximum observed spawners in each spawner-recruit time-series. This was done to constrain the parameter space towards biologically realistic scales - especially given that there is a notable intrinsic correlation between estimates of capacity and productivity (see below; Fig. S16). In the hiearchical models, capacity for each stock is drawn as from a normal distribution (with a lower bound of zero) with a mean set to one half of the maximum observed spawners, and a standard deviation that is double the maximum observed spawner estimate. In practice, this means we approximately that we expect a ~67% probability that the true value of $S_{max}$ ranges from zero to 2.5x maximum spawners, and a ~5% probability it is up to 6x maximum spawners.

To assess whether these priors are justifiable, we applied Maximum Likelihood Estimates of the standard Ricker model (with 1-year autocorrelation) to each spawner-recruit series individually using Template Model Builder (TMB). We subsequently estimate the ratio of this prior-free $S_{max}$ to the maximum observed spawners in each series to yield this distribution. Note that some stocks were trimmed that had extreme ratios (~2%, >10x maximum observed spawners), highlighting the advantage of informative priors in these cases.

```{r, s-smax ratio}

smax.df=data.frame(max.S=NA,smax=NA,ratio=NA,stock=stock_info$stock.name)

for(i in 1:nrow(stock_info)){
  s=subset(stock_dat,stock.id==i)
  
  df=data.frame(S=s$spawners,R=s$recruits,logRS=log(s$recruits/s$spawners))
  ric=samEst::ricker_TMB(df,AC=T,priors_flag=0,silent=T)

  smax.df[i,1]=max(s$spawners)
  smax.df[i,2]=ric$Smax
  smax.df[i,3]=smax.df[i,2]/smax.df[i,1]
  }

par(mfrow=c(1,1))
smax.df2=subset(smax.df,smax.df$ratio<20)
hist(smax.df2[,3],breaks=30,xlab='Ratio of Smax-to-max(S)',main='',ylab='Number of stocks')

print(paste(c(nrow(smax.df)-nrow(smax.df2)),' stock estimates excluded from plot (ratio >10x)',sep=''))
```


# Comparison of random walk vs. GAM nonstationary formulations

We considered an alternative parameterization of the multi-stock nonstationary dynamics model based upon a hierarchical generalized additive model. In this framework, the stock-specific intrinsic productivity at each time-step (ie. $log \alpha_{j,t}$) is a hierarchical deviation from shared ocean region ($log \alpha_{or,t}$) and global estimates ($log \alpha_{0,t}$〗). In the GAM framework, time-varying productivity estimates emerge as the product of a B-spline design matrix of $K$ basis functions representing the span of observed brood cohort years ($B_{t,k}$) and $K$ spline coefficients at stock-specific ($\omega_{j,k}$), ocean region ($\omega_{or,k}$), and global population scales ($\omega_{0,k}$) that are drawn from nested hierarchical distributions, which acts to smooth the spline coefficients and penalize overfitting (Wand 2003). 

$$log(R_{j,t}/S_{j,t}) = log \alpha_{j,t} - S_{j,t}/S_{max,j} + \epsilon_{j,t}$$
$$log \alpha_{j,t} = log \alpha_{j} + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_{j,k} \times B_{t,k}$$
$$log \alpha_{or,t} = log \alpha_{or} + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_{or,k} \times B_{t,k}$$
$$log \alpha_{0,t} = log \alpha_{0} + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_{0,k} \times B_{t,k}$$
$$log \alpha_{j} \sim N(log \alpha_{sr}, \sigma_{\alpha,j})$$
$$log \alpha_{sr} \sim N(log \alpha_{or}, \sigma_{\alpha,sr})$$
$$log \alpha_{or} \sim N(log \alpha_{0}, \sigma_{\alpha,or})$$
$$log \alpha_{0} \sim N(1.5, 4)$$
$$\omega_{j,k} \sim N(\omega_{or,k}, \sigma_{\omega,j})$$
$$\omega_{or,k} \sim N(\omega_{0,k}, \sigma_{\omega,or})$$
$$\omega_{0,k} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\omega})$$
$$S_{max,j} \sim N(0.5 \times max(S_{j,t}), (2 \times max(S_{j,t})))$$
$$\epsilon_{j,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{v,j})$$
$$\sigma_{\alpha,j}/\sigma_{\alpha,sr}/\sigma_{\alpha,or} \sim N(0, 1)$$
$$\sigma_{\omega,j}/\sigma_{\omega,or}/\sigma_{\omega} \sim N(0, 1)$$
$$\sigma_{v,j} \sim Gamma(2, 1)$$

The piecewise polynomials generated in the $N \times K$ B-spline design matrix ($B_{t,k}$) can be set at varying polynomial degrees (e.g. linear, quadratic, cubic, etc.), and the number and placement of the knots can also influence the resulting smoothed function. We generated B-spline matrices using the splines R package with cubic polynomials, which are commonly used in GAMs (Ward et al. 2022), at every 2 years from the beginning to end of the entire brood cohort series for each species to compare to the multi-stock independent random walk model presented in the main manuscript.


```{r,gam vs rw model comp - model load}
gam.chm=readRDS(here('outputs','model fits','gam_fit_chum_k2.RDS'))
rw.chm=readRDS(here('outputs','model fits','ns_fit_chum.RDS'))

loga.chm.rw=rw.chm$draws(variable='log_a_t',format='draws_matrix')
loga.chm.gam=gam.chm$draws(variable='log_a_jt',format='draws_matrix')
muloga.chm.gam=gam.chm$draws(variable='log_a_t',format='draws_matrix')

mloga.chm=apply(muloga.chm.gam,2,median)
```

## Fig. S3 - GAM vs. random walk comparison

Stock-specific productivity (log$\alpha_{j,t}$) trajectories from either individual random walks (A: model presented in main results) or from a hierarchical GAM model (B). Lines indicate median posterior estimates.

```{r,gam vs rw model comp - stock-level,chum,fig.width=6,fig.height=8}
par(mfrow=c(2,1),mar=c(5.1,4.1,2.1,2.1))
plot(mloga.chm~seq(min(chm.info$begin),max(chm.info$end)),ylim=c(0,10),lwd=3,xlab='',type='n',main='',xlim=c(1950,2020),font.axis=2,ylab='',bty='l')
for(j in 1:nrow(chm.info)){
  logaj=apply(loga.chm.rw[,grepl(paste(',',j,']',sep=''),colnames(loga.chm.rw))],2,median)
  lines(exp(logaj)~seq(min(chm.info$begin),max(chm.info$end)),lty=3,col=adjustcolor('black',alpha.f=0.4),lwd=0.5)
  st=chm.info$begin[j]-min(chm.info$begin)+1
  end=chm.info$end[j]-min(chm.info$begin)+1
  lines(exp(logaj[st:end])~seq(chm.info$begin[j],chm.info$end[j]),col=adjustcolor('darkgray',alpha.f=0.8),lwd=0.5)
}
mtext(expression(bold('A')),side=3,adj=0,line=0.5,cex=0.75)
mtext(expression(bold(paste('Productivity (', alpha['j,t'],')',sep=' '))),side=2,adj=0.5,line=2,cex=0.75)
mtext(side=3, adj=0.5,line=1,  expression(bold('Individual random walk estimates')))

plot(mloga.chm~seq(min(chm.info$begin),max(chm.info$end)),ylim=c(0,10),lwd=3,xlab='',type='n',main='',xlim=c(1950,2020),font.axis=2,ylab='',bty='l')
for(j in 1:nrow(chm.info)){
  logaj=apply(loga.chm.gam[,grepl(paste(',',j,']',sep=''),colnames(loga.chm.gam))],2,median)
  lines(exp(logaj)~seq(min(chm.info$begin),max(chm.info$end)),lty=3,col=adjustcolor('black',alpha.f=0.4),lwd=0.5)
  st=chm.info$begin[j]-min(chm.info$begin)+1
  end=chm.info$end[j]-min(chm.info$begin)+1
  lines(exp(logaj[st:end])~seq(chm.info$begin[j],chm.info$end[j]),col=adjustcolor('darkgray',alpha.f=0.8),lwd=0.5)
}
mtext(expression(bold('B')),side=3,adj=0,line=0.5,cex=0.75)
mtext(expression(bold(paste('Productivity (', alpha['j,t'],')',sep=' '))),side=2,adj=0.5,line=2,cex=0.75)
mtext(side=3, adj=0.5,line=1, expression(bold('Hierarchical GAM estimates')))




```

Comparison of the variance in stock-level productivity trajectories for all Chum stocks estimated with either - individual stock-specific random walks in intrinsic productivity (A; following the methodology presented in the main manuscript) or hierarchically estimated deviations from shared GAM estimates (B; as per the formulation above). Each line represents the median estimate of productivity for an individual stock, dotted lines indicate time periods without observations for that particular time-series.

## Fig. S4- GAM vs. random walk comparison by ocean region

Comparison of productivity trajectories by ocean region for Chum salmon comparing population mean productivity estimates by region (A; following the methodology presented in the main manuscript) or hierarchically estimated deviations from a global GAM estimate (B; as per the formulation above). Shading indicates 90% highest posterior density intervals for the mean trajectory and the bold lines represent the median estimates. The transparency of the bold line reflects the proportion of time-series with observations in a given year.

```{r,gam vs rw model comp, chm - ocean region,fig.width=6,fig.height=8}
#
get_samples_by_year <- function(data, year_col, series_id, value, max) {
  # Group by year and count non-NA observations per year
  library(dplyr)
  samples_by_year <- data %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!sym(year_col)) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(SampleCount = sum(!is.na(.data[[value]])), .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::rename(Year = !!sym(year_col))
  samples_by_year$frac=samples_by_year$SampleCount/max
  return(samples_by_year)
}

umsyCalc <- function(a) {
  #gives the min Ricker log-likelihood
  umsy <- (1 - gsl::lambert_W0(exp(1 - a)))
  
  return(umsy)
}
```

From these visualizations we can determine several things. First, that the GAM implementation of the nonstationary dynamics model significantly reduces stock-level variability in productivity trajectories through the hierarchical piece-wise polynomials (Fig. S3). This results in unobserved parts of the inferences (ie. where no observations exist for a stock in a given year) closely following the population mean for those stocks that were observed (see the dotted portions of the median estimates in Fig. S3). The result is that group-level inferences, such as the hierarchical means estimated by ocean region , from the GAM framework are much more variable over time when compared to mean estimates of the individual random walks (Fig. S4). This reflects the partial pooling of the hierarchical estimates being more liable to shift based on the observed samples. For this reason, we believe that the means of the individual random walk model is a more conservative estimate of productivity change - as it assumes, in the absence of evidence (observations), no change in the missing time-series rather than change proportional to the observed series for that period.

The nature of the Ricker model itself is partly why these broad discrepancies in estimates between model forms can exist concurrently. Since the productivity parameter is fairly strongly correlated with the density-dependence parameter ($S_{max}$; see Fig. S21 below), large changes in productivity can be compensated by adjusting $S_{max}$ to come to a similar prediction. We can see this is broadly occurring for these two model forms by comparing their stock-specificestimates of $S_{max}$:

## Fig. S5 - Smax comparison between GAM and random walk

```{r,gam vs rw model comp - smax comp}
smax.chm.rw=rw.chm$draws(variable='Smax',format='draws_matrix')
smax.chm.gam=gam.chm$draws(variable='Smax',format='draws_matrix')

par(mfrow=c(1,1))
plot(apply(log10(smax.chm.gam),2,median)~apply(log10(smax.chm.rw),2,median),yaxt='n',xaxt='n',bty='l',font.axis=2,ylab='',xlab='',pch=21,cex=1.5,bg=adjustcolor('darkgray',alpha.f=0.5))
abline(c(0,1),lwd=2)
pow <- 0:7
ticksat <- as.vector(sapply(pow, function(p) (1:10)*10^p))
axis(1, log10(ticksat), col="black", labels=NA,
     tcl=-0.2, lwd=0, lwd.ticks=1)
axis(1, col="black", at=seq(0,8,by=1),   tcl=-0.45, cex.axis=1.2,
     labels=c(expression(1),expression(10),expression(100),expression('1K'),expression('10K'),expression('100K'),expression('1M'),expression('10M'),expression('100M')))
axis(2, log10(ticksat), col="black", labels=NA,
     tcl=-0.2, lwd=0, lwd.ticks=1)
axis(2, col="black", at=seq(0,8,by=1),   tcl=-0.45, cex.axis=1.2,
     labels=c(expression(1),expression(10),expression(100),expression('1K'),expression('10K'),expression('100K'),expression('1M'),expression('10M'),expression('100M')))
mtext(expression(bold('Smax (random walk)')),side=1,adj=0.5,line=2.5)
mtext(expression(bold('Smax (GAM)')),side=2,adj=0.5,line=2.5)

summary(apply(smax.chm.gam,2,median)/apply(smax.chm.rw,2,median))
```

In this case, the GAM estimates for $S_{max}$ are typically larger (mean ~25%, median ~13%) compared to the individual random walk model.


## Table S2. Recent mean productivity (last 10 brood cohorts) and Umsy by sub-region

Mean productivity (in units of log(R/S)), and standard deviation of mean productivity, for last 10 brood cohorts for each species by sub-region: Chinook (2010-2020), Sockeye (2009-2019), Chum (2010-2020), Coho (2006-2016), even-year Pink (2014-2024), odd-year Pink (2013-2023).

```{r, recent prod table}
    logat2=loga.t.pko[,grepl(paste(seq(c(L-9),L),',',grp[n],']',sep='',collapse = "|"),colnames(loga.t.pko))]
    logat=cbind(logat,logat2)
  }
reg.alpha.dat.pko$mean.logalpha[match(levels(factor(pko.info$region))[r],reg.alpha.dat.pko$region)]=mean(apply(logat,1,mean))
  reg.alpha.dat.pko$sd.logalpha[match(levels(factor(pko.info$region))[r],reg.alpha.dat.pko$region)]=sd(apply(logat,1,mean))
  reg.alpha.dat.pko$mean.umsy[match(levels(factor(pko.info$region))[r],reg.alpha.dat.pko$region)]=samEst::umsyCalc(mean(apply(logat,1,mean)))
  }

df=rbind(reg.alpha.dat.chk,reg.alpha.dat.scy,reg.alpha.dat.chm,reg.alpha.dat.cho,reg.alpha.dat.pke,reg.alpha.dat.pko)

knitr::kable(df, digits=2)
```

```{r, prod trend table}

              n=lme.n[,3],
```

Estimates of annual changes in productivity by stock (calculated as % change in $log(\alpha)$), for each species, as a function of stock size, as measured by $S_{max}$. $r$ indicates the median correlation and 90% highest posterior density intervals between the posteriors of both quantities.

# Static model - stock parameters

For each species, we fit a multi-stock Ricker spawner-recruit model with static parameters (model 1 in main text). Stock-specific productivity ($\alpha_j$) is hierarchically structured based on geography (ie. stocks are nested within sub-regions, which are nested within ocean regions, which are nested in a coastwide estimate). All other parameters are sampled independently for each stock. We present the distributions for each key parameter summarized at different population scales, as these can serve as useful priors in data-limited systems.

## Table S3. Ocean Basin Productivity

Posterior estimates of mean productivity, log($\alpha$), by ocean region for each Pacific salmon species. mean = mean of posterior, sd = standard deviation of posterior.


```{r, or log a table}

df=data.frame(species=c(rep('Chinook',4),rep('Chum',4),rep('Coho',3),rep('Pink (even)',4),rep('Pink (odd)',4),rep('Sockeye',4)),ocean.region=c(rep(c('South Coast','North Coast','Gulf of Alaska','Bering Sea'),2),c('South Coast','North Coast','Gulf of Alaska'),rep(c('South Coast','North Coast','Gulf of Alaska','Bering Sea'),3)),
              n=lme.n[,3],
              mean=c(round(apply(lme.alpha.chk,2,mean),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.chm,2,mean),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.cho,2,mean),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.pke,2,mean),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.pko,2,mean),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.scy,2,mean),2)),
            sd=c(round(apply(lme.alpha.chk,2,sd),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.chm,2,sd),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.cho,2,sd),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.pke,2,sd),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.pko,2,sd),2),round(apply(lme.alpha.scy,2,sd),2)))
```

## Sub-Regional Productivity

Figures S5-S10. Mean productivity, log($\alpha$), estimated for all sub-regions, representing either shared large watersheds or adjacent coastal areas, for each species. Vertical lines indicate the posterior median value and the numbers in parenthesis for each region indicate the stock sample size.

Tables S2-S7. Estimates of mean productivity, log($\alpha$), by sub-region for each species, including the posterior mean (mean), the standard deviation of the mean (sd).

## Fig. S14. Variance in productivity across spatial scales

The proportional variances for differences in the productivity parameter, log($\alpha$), at each hierarchical spatial scale, representing the median estimates of $\sigma^2$ relative to their sum from the static hierarchical model (eq. 1).

```{r, log a variance}
alpha.chk.var=stc.chk$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')
alpha.scy.var=stc.scy$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')
alpha.chm.var=stc.chm$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')
alpha.cho.var=stc.cho$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')
alpha.pke.var=stc.pke$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')
alpha.pko.var=stc.pko$draws(variable=c('sd_a_or','sd_a_sr','sd_a'),format='draws_matrix')


df=data.frame(species=c(rep('Chinook',3),rep('Sockeye',3),rep('Chum',3),rep('Coho',3),rep('Pink - Even',3),rep('Pink - odd',3)),percent.var=c(apply(alpha.chk.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.chk.var^2,2,median)),apply(alpha.scy.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.scy.var^2,2,median)),apply(alpha.chm.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.chm.var^2,2,median)),apply(alpha.cho.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.cho.var^2,2,median)),apply(alpha.pke.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.pke.var^2,2,median)),apply(alpha.pko.var^2,2,median)/sum(apply(alpha.pko.var^2,2,median))),scale=c(rep(c('Ocean Region','Sub-Region','Stock-specific'))))
df$scale=factor(df$scale,levels=c('Ocean Region','Sub-Region','Stock-specific'))

ggplot(df, aes(fill=scale, y=percent.var, x=species))+
  scale_fill_manual(values=RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3,'Blues'),name='Spatial scale')+ 
  geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity") + theme_minimal() +
xlab('')+ylab('Proportional variance in long-term productivity')+
            theme(panel.background = element_blank(),strip.background = element_rect(colour=NA, fill=NA),panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, color = "black"),
                  strip.text = element_text(face="bold", size=12),
                  axis.text=element_text(face="bold"),axis.title = element_text(face="bold"),plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5,size=15),legend.position = "right",axis.text.x = element_text(
      color = c(sp_cols[1,1],sp_cols[2,1],sp_cols[3,1],sp_cols[4,1],sp_cols[4,1],sp_cols[5,1])))


knitr::kable(df)

```

## Fig. S15. Smax posteriors by species

```{r, smax,fig.dim = c(6, 8)}

par(mfrow=c(3,2))
par(mar=c(3,5,3,1))
ymax=max(hist(apply(log10(smax.scy),2,median),plot=FALSE)$counts)

axis(1, col="black", at=seq(0,8,by=1),   tcl=-0.45, cex.axis=1.2,
```

\newpage

## Parameter correlations

This section examines the correlation between estimates of different spawner-recruit parameters including stock productivity (log($\alpha$)),  capacity ($Smax$), and recruitment deviance ($sigma$). We show correlations both across stocks, which tests for potential scaling relationships (ie. are larger stocks more or less productive or variable), and within the posterior sample for each stock, which gives an indication of the intrinsic correlation between intercepts and slopes in the estimation of the Ricker spawner-recruit model.


```{r, correlations in a and b}
alphas.chk=stc.chk$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')
alphas.scy=stc.scy$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')
alphas.chm=stc.chm$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')
alphas.cho=stc.cho$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')
alphas.pke=stc.pke$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')
alphas.pko=stc.pko$draws(variables='log_a',format='draws_matrix')

corr.across.chk=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.chk)){
  corr.across.chk[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.chk[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.chk[i,])))
}
corr.within.chk=NA
for(i in 1:ncol(alphas.chk)){
  corr.within.chk[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.chk[,i]),as.vector(log(smax.chk[,i])))
}

corr.across.scy=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.scy)){
  corr.across.scy[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.scy[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.scy[i,])))
}
corr.within.scy=NA
for(i in 1:ncol(alphas.scy)){
  corr.within.scy[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.scy[,i]),as.vector(log(smax.scy[,i])))
}

corr.across.chm=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.chm)){
  corr.across.chm[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.chm[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.chm[i,])))
}
corr.within.chm=NA
for(i in 1:ncol(alphas.chm)){
  corr.within.chm[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.chm[,i]),as.vector(log(smax.chm[,i])))
}

corr.across.cho=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.cho)){
  corr.across.cho[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.cho[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.cho[i,])))
}
corr.within.cho=NA
for(i in 1:ncol(alphas.cho)){
  corr.within.cho[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.cho[,i]),as.vector(log(smax.cho[,i])))
}

corr.across.pke=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.pke)){
  corr.across.pke[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.pke[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.pke[i,])))
}
corr.within.pke=NA
for(i in 1:ncol(alphas.pke)){
  corr.within.pke[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.pke[,i]),as.vector(log(smax.pke[,i])))
}

corr.across.pko=NA
for(i in 1:nrow(alphas.pko)){
  corr.across.pko[i]=cor(as.vector(alphas.pko[i,]),as.vector(log(smax.pko[i,])))
}
corr.within.pko=NA

}
```
